newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy minister denies mass pension cutback planned.
newsitem.headline: Italy minister denies mass pension cutback planned.

text.p: Italian Regional Affairs Minister Franco Bassanini said on Monday the government was not planning to scrap early retirement for all state sector workers, a suggestion that had infuriated key hard-left allies.
Italy announced last week that it was limiting early retirement for teachers but Bassanini told a news conference that no other sectors would be affected.
"I exclude a block on pensions in other sectors," he said.
"We have adopted a measure on schools...we are not studying others," Bassanini said. "In other sectors there isn't the same emergency."

Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti, whose hard-left party holds the balance of power in the lower house of parliament, had earlier demanded an immediate official denial of reports that wider cuts were planned.
Bertinotti had said that if the centre-left government was planning to extend the freeze to all civil servants, as reported in the news media, Refoundation would refuse its support.

Massimo D'Alema, leader of the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) which is the biggest in Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government, said Italy could not go on with the current system which was unsustainable.
"When there is mass unemployment, especially among the young in the Mezzogiorno (south), we can't allow ourselves to pay pensions at 50 or 52 years of age," D'Alema told a conference.
"This system is increasingly unsustainable. We have to get out of it, it's the only way."
D'Alema also told Reuters Financial Television on Monday that the 1998 budget would include structural reform of the pensions system and the government was working to that end.
Prodi's cabinet on Friday approved a plan to stem the flood of teachers seeking retirement. Only around half of the 65,000 teachers who have requested it will now be given the go-ahead.
A hold-down on early retirements could bring big savings for the cash-strapped Treasury as Italy fights to control state spending to meet targets for the European single currency.
State pensions body Inps has reported a recent surge in requests for early retirements from various sectors amid rising fears of a government crackdown on pension benefits.
The government last week began what are expected to be lengthy talks with union leaders on welfare reform.
Bertinotti is totally opposed to any social spending cuts and has described welfare reform as "the mother of all issues" on which the government will stand or fall.
He said earlier that if the government was seeking to "call into question the right for all state sector employees to take early retirement (it) will not be able to count on its majority.
"The opposition of Communist Refoundation would be very fierce," he said in a statement.
Prodi's centre-left government almost fell in April when Refoundation refused to back a security force for Albania.
Economists say Italy must bite the welfare bullet to have a hope of being in economic and monetary union at its 1999 launch.
Italy spends more than any other European Union country on pension benefits and the bill is set to climb unless reforms are introduced, the statistical institute Istat said last week.

While Italy's total welfare spending is lower than the European Union average, spending on old age pensions was 13 percent of gross domestic product in 1994, almost three percent more than the EU average, Istat said in its annual report.
